Abstract A novel method for the preparation of 3-allenyl-4-methy-
lenetetrahydrofurans vi a a Pd-catalyzed enyne cyclization reaction of
propargyl 2-en-4-ynyl ethers under Suzuki coupling conditions is dis-
closed. The reaction proc eeds via Pd activation of the terminal alkyne,
cyclization, formation of the alleny l moiety, and reductive elimination,
leading to the final product. This methodology offers several advantag-
es, such as easy manipulation, mild reaction conditions, and easily ac-
cessible starting materials, providing a range of trisubstituted and 1,1-
disubstituted allenyl(methylene)furan derivatives.
Key words allenes, furans, propargyl ethers, palladium, cyclization,
Suzuki coupling
Allenyl heterocycles are usef ul synthetic intermediates
due to the potential cyclization of heterocycles with the al-
lenylic moiety to form polycyclic frameworks.1,2 In addition,
such allenyl heterocycles appear in natural products and
pharmaceutical molecules.
2 Thus, development of synthetic
methods for the construction of allenyl heterocycles and
their applications have received much attention.1–3
Synthetic methodologies lead ing to allenyl compounds
are well documented. Among them, Pd-catalyzed reaction
of propargylic compounds I with nucleophilic organome-
tallic or organoboron reagents to give the corresponding al-
lene products is a known procedure (Scheme 1A). 4 In fur-
ther applications, conjugated ( Z)-2-en-4-ynes II behave
similarly to provide the vinylallene products (Scheme 1B). 5
By adopting this concept, we  imagined that a 2-en-4-yl
propargyl ether III with a terminal alkynyl group moiety
could be useful to prepare allenyl(methylene)furans VI
(Scheme 2). Presumably, activation of the terminal alkyne
by Pd gives IV as the primary intermediate. 6 Hopefully, an
intramolecular addition to the enyne moiety followed by
isomerization and protonation at the terminal allenyl car-
bon would take place to provide vinylpalladium species V.
Aryl group transfer from the boron reagent to the Pd center
and then reductive elimination would deliver the target
framework VI.
Scheme 2  A proposed reaction pathway leading to allenyl(methy-
lene)furans
1-En-4-yn-3-ols are useful synthetic intermediates and
readily available from the addition of acetylides to chalcone
molecules.

With the optimized conditions, reactions of various
substituted groups R 1, R2, and R 3 in 1 with various aryl- or

acids smoothly under the catalytic conditions described
above to give the al lenylfuran products 2, except for 1d (R1
= Me) (Table 2, entries 1–4). It appears that these substitu-
ents with different electronic natures affect the yield. When
R1 is a p-nitrophenyl group, the yield of 2b dropped to 55%
(entry 2). Unfortunately, compound 1d with an alkyl sub-
stituent as R 1 did not provide the desired product 2d at all
(entry 4).
As for the boronic acids, phenylboronic acids with an
electron-withdrawing or -donating substituent are suitable
for the reaction, to give 2e and 2f in good yields (entries 5
and 6). However, reaction of 1a with butylboronic acid gave
an unexpected product, 2g (R

group provided the expected product 2k (entry 11). It ap-
pears that the nature of the R 3 substituent affects the reac-
tion significantly.

by formation of the allenyl group to render the desired

(Figure 2) with an internal alkynyl moiety did not undergo

argyl ether, indicating the necessity of the alkynyl function-
ality.
Figure 2  Structures of 1q and 1r
A possible reaction pathway leading to 2 is illustrated in
Scheme 6. Activation of the terminal alkyne of 1 by Pd(0)
results in the formation of Int-1A,6a which then undergoes
nucleophilic attack at the enyne moiety to yield the furan
ring, Int-1B, where R 2 is seated at the pseudo-equatorial
position to avoid steric strain. This orientation of R 2 readily
renders the stereochemistry of the furan ring in the final
product. The allenyl anion in Int-1B is able to accept a pro-
ton from a solvent molecule to give Int-1C. Transmetalation
of the R4 group from R4B(OH)2 to Pd gives the intermediate
Int-1D, which proceeds to undergo reductive elimination to
yield the final product 2. For 1 with R3 as a TMS substituent,
desilylation might take place during the reaction in the for-
mation of 3.

Abstract A novel method for the preparation of 3-allenyl-4-methy-
lenetetrahydrofurans via a Pd-catalyzed enyne cyclization reaction of
propargyl 2-en-4-ynyl ethers under Suzuki coupling conditions is dis-
closed. The reaction proceeds via Pd activation of the terminal alkyne,
cyclization, formation of the allenyl moiety, and reductive elimination,
leading to the final product. This methodology offers several advantag-
es, such as easy manipulation, mild reaction conditions, and easily ac-
cessible starting materials, providing a range of trisubstituted and 1,1-
disubstituted allenyl(methylene)furan derivatives.

Key words allenes, furans, propargyl ethers, palladium, cyclization,
Suzuki coupling

Allenyl heterocycles are useful synthetic intermediates
due to the potential cyclization of heterocycles with the al-
lenylic moiety to form polycyclic frameworks.<sup>1,2</sup> In addition,
such allenyl heterocycles appear in natural products and
pharmaceutical molecules.<sup>2</sup> Thus, development of synthetic
methods for the construction of allenyl heterocycles and
their applications have received much attention.<sup>1–3</sup>

Synthetic methodologies leading to allenyl compounds
are well documented. Among them, Pd-catalyzed reaction
of propargylic compounds I with nucleophilic organome-
tallic or organoboron reagents to give the corresponding al-
lene products is a known procedure (Scheme 1A).<sup>4</sup> In fur-
ther applications, conjugated (Z)-2-en-4-ynes II behave
similarly to provide the vinylallene products (Scheme 1B).<sup>5</sup>

In summary, we have disclosed an efficient method to
prepare 3-allenyl-4-methylenetetrahydrofurans 2 and 3 via
the Pd-catalyzed enyne cyclization reaction of propargyl 2-

starting materials. Further study to extend the application
of allenyl(methylene)furans in synthetic utility is ongoing
in our laboratory.
